content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies large language models' capabilities of picking up causal relations. It is done through analyzing causal question answering capabilities and embeddings similarity of correlations on causal facts. The findings is that LLM might be able to capture causal relations in a form through causal question-answering but no evidence of any underlying causal reasoning.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
	• Designed an analysis means to probe and test whether LLM can capture causal relationships (correlations).
	• The findings that LLMs capture causal relationships (correlations) but not reasoning is of scientific interests.
	

Weakness
	• The definition of CCF needs to be defined formally and explicitly so that the experimental hypotheses (e.g. Q1-Q3) can be defined formally and then we can then prove or dis-prove them by checking a few key verifiable indicators regarding the formal definitions. 
This work is original in terms of proposing a means to understand aspects of  causality that is captured in LLM. The quality and clarity of the technical content needs to be improved to make the methodology and conclusions more formal and explicit.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This work is original in terms of proposing a means to understand aspects of  causality that is captured in LLM. The quality and clarity of the technical content needs to be improved to make the methodology and conclusions more formal and explicit.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This work is on an important issue of LLM in terms of its capability of capturing causality. The results are interesting in terms of finding that causal relationship is captured in a form but no evidence of causal reasoning. The description of the methodology is intuitive but lacking formal treatment rendering the analysis results and findings less rigorous.  

Details
	1. Page 4, please define causal facts here to make this paper self-contained; also define causal relationships and performing intervention formally here to be self-contained; more important the definition of the formal concept of "correlations of causal facts".
	2. Page 4, " To further ensure stability of the results, manual proofs reading is conducted", please detail the process so that the readers can verify how this process might affect the validity of the study.
	3. Page 4, please make Q1-Q3 more formally and explicitly along with formal qualitive or quantitative measures of these hypotheses so that can be verified formally and their experiments can be validated formally.
	4. Page 7, missing words: "we compare the to the embedding of say …"
	5. Page 7-8, the experiment section might be restructured to clearly go through Q1-Q3 hypotheses along with the corresponding experiments, the results and the conclusions on them. Materials such as prototype prediction and statement embedding definitions can be taken out of the experiments to make the experiment reporting regarding Q1-Q3 more clear.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper analyzes whether large language models pick up correlations between queries posed to them and their answers.
They propose that models showcase "correlations of causal facts (CCF)". They analyze this by directly probing causal or non-causal relationships between different variables, by expressing them in natural language (for e.g., "Does X cause Y?") and constructing a graph based on the model predictions. They study three questions: 1) how well do LMs recover partially known causal graphs?, 2) how do LMs perform in commonsense settings?, and 3) how do synonyms or name perturbations affect LM estimates?
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

- The paper considers an interesting analysis question, looking at whether LLMs reason causally or whether they operate primarily based on statistical correlations.

Weaknesses:

- There is too much philosophical content throughout the paper, which does not contribute to the understanding of the reader. Further, the paper often refers to social media conversations and quotes them as evidence for different stances. This doesn't conform with scientific writing and seems extremely odd.

- The empirical analysis conducted in this work is not justified. I am unsure why phrasing candidate causal relationships in natural language and taking these predictions as is, is a suitable way of probing whether models capture causality. 

- The research questions proposed in this work are far too vague. In addition, there are no medium to large-scale experiments conducted in the paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper needs significant work on all fronts: experiments, technique and writing. I would suggest removing content that discusses stances on philosophical debates about the future of AI, and instead focusing on concrete research questions, that are meaningfully explored.

I would also suggest reading Elazar et al 2022 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.14251) as it seems relevant to the discussion.

Typos:
- Abstract: "LLMs" are

I would strongly suggest reviewing relevant work and proposing the same questions with thorough empirical investigations, and concretely posed research questions.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper tries to understand whether large language models capture factual information in the world. The authors use probing to look for correlations between words that have causal relationships in reality. Using that approach, they show that causal facts are correlated in the embedding space.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
This paper touches on a central problem in deep learning: do models capture causal relationships between objects in the world. The authors try to link ideas from causal inference to understand what information large language models capture, which is an important and timely problem.

Weaknesses:

While I whole-heartedly share the intuition of the authors that causal inference is the way to understand how large language models make decisions, I find this paper in its current form to be highly problematic and outright misleading.

Starting from the very first sentence, the authors make strong unsupported claims. In fact, the abstract starts off with a very strong claim which I disagree on. This artificial divide made by the authors, putting the research community in two opposing camps seems factually incorrect. It’s not that the argument against AGI and scaling is lack of interpretability. No one is claiming that DNNs are interpretable. Also, what are causal representations? There seems to be some confusion throughout the paper between causal representation learning, a field within causal machine learning that uses tools from causal inference to learn robust and interpretable models, and the factuality of the information held within trained LLms. Generally, I think that the paper should be rewritten for better readability, and without grandiose claims in the abstract (and throughout the paper).

Also, and more importantly, probing was shown extensively to fail in capturing what language models know (see missing references). I suggest the authors use a more faithful (and hopefully causal) method for understanding how deep neural networks (including large language models) make decisions. In its current form, the experimental setup simply does not allow inferring any causal relationships in the trained model. This is a model interpretability problem, but the authors completely disregard the vast literature on model explanations in NLP.

More broadly, this paper reads more as an opinion piece regarding recent advances in AI, not as a research paper on a clear problem. The authors often cite opinions made on social media, all while failing to address the actual research on this important and widely studied topic. Citing Pearl is not a substitute for doing actual causal inference.

The authors also completely ignore the vast literature on causal inference and natural language processing, claiming they are the first to: “investigate the question in its presented form”, meaning the causal foundations of decisions made by trained language models. I highly recommend the authors check out the references attached to this review to educate themselves on this vast and quickly expanding literature.

Asking a few statements about trivial causal relationships in the world does not settle the “heated debate around AI”. It just serves as some anecdotal evidence that models capture information about the world. In citing so many causal inference papers, I would expect the authors to show more humility in trying to estimate causal effects.

Some examples of missing references:


1. Causal inference in natural language processing: Estimation, prediction, interpretation and beyond
2. Counterfactual invariance to spurious correlations in text classification
3. CausaLM: Causal model explanation through counterfactual language models
4. Invariant Risk Minimization
5. CEBaB: Estimating the Causal Effects of Real-World Concepts on NLP Model Behavior
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Please see complete discussion under weaknesses. 

In brief, this paper makes strong claims about causal relationships held within large language models. The study is deeply flawed and completely disregards the vast literature on the topic. It does provide reproducible results, but the findings are not novel and do not allow answering the posed research questions.
content.summary_of_the_review: While I whole-heartedly share the intuition of the authors that causal inference is the way to understand how large language models make decisions, I find this paper in its current form to be highly problematic and outright misleading. This paper reads more as an opinion piece regarding recent advances in AI, not as a research paper on a clear problem. The authors completely ignore the vast literature on causal inference and natural language processing. This is especially problematic given that the method the authors use was shown to fail in capturing what language models know.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper conducts tests on large language models aimed at assessing the models' understanding of causal facts. As I'll detail below, the methodological descriptions are lacking in detail and clarity, but it seems that the experiments include inspection of models' generated text in response to prompts stating causal relations, as well as cosine computations between sentence embeddings for causal statements and other "prototype" embeddings. The authors make assorted observations about the results, including instability of the "knowledge" in face of variation in phrasing.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: The paper aims to contribute to better understanding the linguistic capabilities of LLMs, in the interesting and relevant domain of causal relations.

Weaknesses: The paper is written with very non-standard structure and prioritization of content (at least within the AI/ML/NLP community). In particular, it spends an inordinate amount of time (as much as half the paper) on quite high-level, abstract, fairly wandering philosophical discussion and broad overview of debates surrounding understanding in LLMs, "foundation models", etc. By contrast, the Related Work section consists of a single brief paragraph, and when the paper finally reaches the description of the experiments that it contributes, the description of methods is sparse, haphazard, and far from complete. Instead, it seems the experimental sections focus almost exclusively on high-level characterization of the questions the authors intend to ask with their tests, followed by sets of assorted observations that don't feel particularly systematic, comprehensive, or grounded in specific hypotheses. 

The result is that the submission has two major problems:

1) The paper feels far from adequately anchored in the current literature. Consider the representative excerpt: 

"Since we want to query the large language model for what it has learned, while unfortunately being unable to directly measure the expected 'correlations of causal facts', we resort to indirect measurements by simply querying the black box system systematically. In a sense, it is the analogue procedure of what the community around explainable AI in computer vision, that is, 'opening the black box' by attributing to the input the changes it caused on the output."

With these sentences the authors frame their contribution in a way that suggests they are largely unaware of (or at least not engaged with) the massive and continually growing analysis/interpretation/explanation literature in NLP. This issue is further reflected in the lack of acknowledgement of that literature in the overview of related work, and in the simplistic nature of the testing methods used (and lack of comparison of those methods against the many, many analysis methods that are already being used).

2) The methods are far from adequately described, but from what I can infer they are simplistic, not particularly well-motivated, and don't reflect any obvious effort to control the quality/precision of the tests. In the first part it seems like the authors basically took collections of causal statements and input them to the models and then made observations about what the models generated in response. In the second part the authors lay out some not-terribly-transparent reasoning which leads them to compute cosine similarities between a) sentence embeddings and b) some True/False prototype embeddings the derivation of which is unclear (but which might be an average of True/False statements, from somewhere). There is no discussion of any measures taken to try to control the test data to avoid influence of confounds, heuristics, etc. The paper includes some assorted figures of causal graphs which are intended to reflect results from the experiments, but there is no clear indication of the procedure by which the graphs are derived from the model outputs/cosine similarities. The authors mention publicly available datasets that they draw their inputs from, but they give no description of what these datasets are. Methodological clarity issues were present throughout, but sections that I noted in which the opacity was particularly severe were Section 3.3, and the final paragraph before the Conclusion section. I really have no idea what is going on in either of those excerpts. 

The critical unanswered questions here are so numerous that I don't think it's practical to try to lay them all out here -- so I'll just try to summarize: to assess the methods used here, for the first set of experiments readers must know precisely what the input data to the models was, exactly how it was input, exactly what kind of output was assessed, and by what procedure/criteria that assessment was done. For the second set of experiments, we need to know what sentences were being embedded for testing, and exactly what data and procedure produced the prototype vectors. And for all experiments, there needs to be a clear explanation of the linking computations between the model results and the graph structures being displayed. All methods furthermore need to be compared against existing analysis methods in the literature, and it is within that context that an argument must be made for the adequacy and novelty of the current contribution. Results should also be presented comprehensively, in tables or figures, rather than with sporadic observations about individual models and presentation of individual example graphs.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: As I've outlined above, there are substantial issues with clarity, quality, novelty, and reproducibility in this submission -- I believe what I've said above should cover what I would reiterate here.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper sets out with entirely reasonable goals in terms of better understanding LLMs, but it fails to engage with the massive existing analysis/interpretation/explanation literature in NLP, and it presents analyses that seem simplistic and inadequately motivated -- though due to severe issues in methodological clarity, judging this requires a fair amount of guesswork. I hope that the authors will properly engage with the existing analysis literature, and update their experimental methods (as appropriate) and reporting of the experiments accordingly, for future versions of this work.

content.title: Probing for Correlations of Causal Facts: Large Language Models and Causality
content.TL;DR: We hypothesize that LLMs exploit correlations between the questions on causal relations with their expected (or "right") causal answers.
content.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are subject to an ongoing heated debate, leaving open the question of progress towards AGI and dividing the community into two camps: the ones who see the arguably impressive results as evidence to the scaling hypothesis, and the others who are worried about the lack of interpretability and reasoning capabilities. By investigating to which extent causal representations might be captured by LLMs, we make a humble effort towards resolving the ongoing philosophical conflicts. We hypothesize that causal facts are part of the training data and that the LLM are capable of picking up correlations between the questions on causal relations with their expected (or ``right'') causal answers. We study this hypothesis two-fold, (1) by analyzing the LLM's causal question answering capabilities and (2) by probing the LLM's embeddings for correlations on the causal facts. Our analyses suggests that LLMs are somewhat capable of answering causal queries the right way through memorization of the corresponding question-answer pair. However, more importantly, the evidence suggests that LLMs do not perform causal reasoning to arrive at their answers.
